1107.title: Heaven
1107.hook: less clouds and harps, more being with God and all things made new
1107.howItsDone: Christians speak of heaven at funerals, in the creeds' "life of the world to come", and in hymns; the Bible's own descriptions come chiefly from Revelation 21–22 and from Jesus's and Paul's promises of being with Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purgatory, and how the churches remember their dead. Your line was mercy after death.

Clouds. Harps. Someone in a white robe at a gate, checking names off a list. The cartoon heaven is so familiar it's hard to see past it. And some of it does come from the Bible: the book of Revelation has harps, and white robes, and gates of pearl. But when the Bible's last pages describe the end of the story, the center of the picture isn't the furniture. It's a person, and one small word that keeps coming back.

Here's how Revelation describes the end: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them." With, and with, and with. Then: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death." And notice which way things move. Not souls floating up and away, but a holy city coming down, and the one on the throne saying, "Behold, I make all things new." John sees "a new heaven and a new earth": this world healed, not thrown out. The same small word runs through the rest. On the cross, a dying thief says, "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." And he hears: "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Paul, writing from prison, says he'd like "to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better." And to grieving friends in Thessalonica he says, "and so shall we ever be with the Lord." The churches have their own ways of saying more. Catholics speak of the beatific vision: seeing God face to face. The Orthodox speak of union with God that keeps on deepening, without end. Protestant hymns sing of home, and rest, and the face of Christ. But in these passages the shorthand is simple: heaven is where God is, and the hope they voice is to be with him.
screen: `THE TABERNACLE OF GOD IS WITH MEN.`

segments.voice: Bring back one moment of real joy: a table full of people you love, a morning by the sea, a child laughing until they can't stop. Then take away the shadow that often comes with joy, the knowing that it will end: no clock, no goodbyes, nothing lost. If you pray, thank God for that hope; if you don't, just rest in the shape of it.
Heaven. In the Bible's last pages, less a place above the clouds than God living with his people, and all things made new.
Your line: with him. Not the furniture; the company. I'll be here tomorrow.

1108.title: Hell
1108.hook: traditions teach eternal separation; some hold that the lost cease to be; some hope all may be saved
1108.howItsDone: Christians meet the teaching on hell in the Gospels' warnings and in the creeds' judgment of the living and the dead; Catholic and Orthodox teaching and the classic Protestant confessions hold it as real and lasting separation from God, while some Christians hold other views.

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaven, and the small word at its center. Your line was with him.

Near Jerusalem lies a valley. The Bible calls it the valley of the son of Hinnom, and Jeremiah says a terrible thing was done there: children burned in the fire, something God says he never commanded. When Jesus warns about hell in Matthew, the Greek word is Gehenna, and readers trace it to that valley's name. On that reading, a real place of horror became the name for final loss. It's a hard subject, and the churches hold it in more than one way.

Start with what Jesus says, because he says it seriously. In Matthew, after the sheep and the goats are separated: "these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal." And elsewhere he says to fear the one "which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." Catholic and Orthodox teaching, and the classic Protestant confessions, hold that hell is real and lasting: separation from God. Catholic teaching describes it as a person's own final choice to shut God out, not God's wish. Some Christians read that other line, destroy both soul and body, and hold that the lost finally cease to be. The fire, they say, is final, not endless. And some Christians, including some Orthodox writers, hope that God's love may in the end reach everyone. They lean on Paul, who says God "will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth." They hold it as a hope, not a promise. These readings disagree, and the disagreement matters. But they share two things. Each takes evil and its cost seriously. And each reads the same verse about God's heart. Peter writes that the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." On that verse, no one's loss is what God wants. An old hymn puts it in a line: "There's a wideness in God's mercy."

Start close, with the people in your home and the people you'll see today, then widen to your street, your city, people you'll never meet. Then the hard ones, someone who hurt you, someone whose choices you can't understand, without arguing over whether they deserve it. If you pray, bring them before God, the way Paul asks prayers to be made for all; if you don't, wish each one well, as widely as you can reach.
Hell. In the Gospels, Gehenna: a word readers trace to a valley's name, used for final loss. Churches read it as lasting separation, as an end, or alongside a hope that all be saved.
Your line: his mercy is wide. Peter's verse, read by every view. See you tomorrow.

1109.title: He will come again
1109.hook: the creeds say Christ will return; churches differ on how and when
1109.howItsDone: Christians who say the Apostles' or Nicene Creed confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and the season of Advent looks toward his coming; churches differ on how they read the details in Revelation and Paul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hell, and the different ways churches hold it. Your line was his mercy is wide.

A group of friends stands on a hill, staring at the sky. Jesus has just been taken up out of their sight, and they're still looking. Then two men in white are beside them: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven." The creeds keep that promise. Churches have read it in different ways: some with urgency, some with quiet patience, some with careful timelines.

The creeds say it in a line. The Apostles' Creed: "From thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead." The quick means the living. One New Testament Greek word for his coming is parousia: an arrival, a presence. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that say the creeds share that hope. Where they differ is how, and when. Revelation speaks of a thousand years in which Christ reigns. Some read that as a future age that begins when he returns. Others read it as now: the time of the church, between his first coming and his second. Some evangelical churches teach that believers will first be caught up to meet him, often called the rapture, drawing on Paul's words about meeting the Lord in the air. Other churches read those same words differently. And the date? Jesus is plain: "But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." So the stance the Gospels ask for is not calculation but readiness. Jesus tells of servants who keep their lights burning, waiting up for their master. And near the Bible's very end comes a short prayer: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Paul, closing his first letter to Corinth, leaves an Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha. Readers take it two ways: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. Some readers hear both in it: he came, and he will come.

Jesus tells of servants with their lights burning, awake when their master knocks: not frightened, ready. So ask quietly, if today were the day, what would I want to have done, who would I call, what would I put down, and let one answer come clearly. If you pray, use the prayer near the Bible's end, even so, come, Lord Jesus; if you don't, just hold the question.
He will come again. The creeds' promise that Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. Churches share the promise, and differ on how and when.
Your line: come, Lord Jesus. Ready, not frightened: that is the stance asked for. Until next time.

1110.title: In essentials, unity
1110.hook: an old motto: in essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity
1110.howItsDone: Christians from different churches can be found working and praying together on what they hold in common, such as the creeds, the Lord's Prayer and service to neighbors, while keeping their own teaching on matters where they differ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he will come again, and a prayer near the Bible's end. Your line was come, Lord Jesus.

In essentials, unity. In non-essentials, liberty. In all things, charity. Three short lines, sometimes lettered on a church wall or printed in a bulletin. People like to hang the motto on famous names; who first wrote it is less certain than the motto itself. What's clear is who it was written for: Christians who disagreed, sometimes bitterly, and still had to share a city, a table, a faith. After a block of honest disagreements, it's a good place to stand.

The idea is older than the motto. Paul faced it in his letter to Rome. Some believers ate meat; others ate only herbs. Some kept certain days as holy; others treated every day alike. They were starting to look down on each other. Paul's answer opens like this: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." Welcome each other, and don't turn the welcome into a debate. And then: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." Food and days, for Paul, were not things to split over. Now the hard part. Who decides what counts as essential? Churches don't share one list. Some point to the creeds. Some to the plain teaching of scripture about Christ. Catholics and Orthodox to the teaching the church has received and handed on. Even the list of essentials is something Christians disagree about. Which is why the last line carries so much weight. In Paul's chapter on love, charity is the King James word for love, and the chapter is blunt: "though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." All faith. Even right faith, on every essential. Without love, nothing. So the letter to the Ephesians asks for effort: "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Unity there isn't a feeling that happens on its own. It's something kept, on purpose.

Choose one real disagreement, with a relative, a friend, a church, a stranger online, and ask: is this essential, or not? Whatever you decide, find one good thing the other person is trying to protect, and hold it a while without giving up your own view. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well.
In essentials. The first line of an old motto: unity on what matters most, liberty on the rest, and charity, which is love, over everything.
Your line: in all things, charity. The motto's last line, and its heaviest. Go gently.

1111.title: Block close: many rooms
1111.hook: the family disagrees, and still says one creed
1111.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed in their worship, and Christians of different churches pray together, especially in shared services for Christian unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in essentials, unity, and an old motto that ends in love. Your line was in all things, charity.

A family can share one house and still argue about the thermostat, the dishes, whose turn it is to cook. Through this whole block of the path, the Christian family has been arguing out loud: about the table, about Mary, about the saints, about images and the dead. No church here was asked to back down, and none did. And yet the Nicene Creed, said in Orthodox, Catholic and other churches, still opens with the same words: I believe in one God. Today the block closes.

This block asked the big questions, and let each church answer in its own voice. It began with words about God: theology, and the way of not-knowing that says what God is not. It asked where authority lives, sola scriptura, scripture alone, or scripture read within the church's tradition, and what it means to call scripture God-breathed. It tried pictures of the Trinity that all fall short, and the filioque, one word in a long argument. Then sin and grace: Augustine and Pelagius, the Reformed comfort of being chosen, Wesley's grace that goes before. The cross from several sides: victory over death, a debt paid, a place taken, a love that changes us. Justified by faith. Made holy. Theosis, becoming like God, iron glowing in the fire. Then the church itself: its marks, its ministers, its water and its table. Mary, the God-bearer. The saints, the images, the dead. Heaven, hell, and the promise of his return. The answers differed, and this block didn't pretend otherwise. But listen to Jesus on his last night, praying for everyone who would believe through his friends: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." And earlier that same evening, to friends who were frightened: "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you." Mansions, in the King James. Dwelling places. Rooms. Many of them, in one house, and room enough for a family that argues.

Bring to mind one person whose faith isn't yours: a Christian from another church, a neighbor from another tradition, a friend who holds no faith. Don't think about where you disagree; think about their face, their week, what they might be carrying. If you pray, ask good things for them in words your tradition gives you; if you don't, wish them peace, warmly.
Block close. The end of the big questions: many answers, honestly different, from one family that still says one creed. Tomorrow a new block begins: traditions of prayer.
Your line: many rooms, one house. I believe in one God, still said together. See you tomorrow.

1112.title: Listen (Rule, Prologue)
1112.hook: the Rule's first word: listen, my son, with the ear of your heart
1112.howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the Rule is read aloud to the community in short passages, and each time through it begins again with the Prologue's call to listen; lay people who follow Benedictine ways, called oblates, may read the Rule at home as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a block close: a family that disagrees and still says one creed. Your line was many rooms, one house.

Ausculta. That's the first word of a short book for monks, written in Latin by a man the church remembers as Saint Benedict. It's called simply the Rule. Before it says a thing about prayer times, food, sleep or work, it says one word. Listen. Not read carefully. Not obey. Listen. And not only with the ears on the side of your head: the opening line asks the reader, as a son, to listen to the teacher's instruction and bend down the ear of the heart. A new block starts today, traditions of prayer, the different ways Christians have learned to pray, and the first house is the Benedictines.

The ear of the heart is an odd phrase, and it's meant to be. An ear hears sounds. This ear goes further in: listening all the way down, willing to be changed by what it hears. The picture is an old one. In Proverbs, a parent says, "My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings." Incline. Lean the ear over, the way you lean toward someone speaking softly in a loud room. A little further on, the Prologue reaches for a psalm about listening too: "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart." Today. Not someday when life is quieter. Now notice what the Rule takes for granted. In its picture, God is already speaking, through scripture, the teacher, the community, the day as it comes, and the trouble is mostly on the listener's end. People are busy. They rehearse their answer. They hear half a sentence and fill in the rest. So the Rule doesn't start with a technique. It starts with a posture: lean in, bend down, leave room for a voice that isn't yours. Prayer times, food, sleep and work all come after. A whole way of life, built on one verb, and anyone can practice it, with or without a cloister: at a kitchen table, in a meeting, on the phone with your mother.
screen: `AN EAR THAT GOES ALL THE WAY IN.`
`TO DAY IF YE WILL HEAR HIS VOICE.`

Your line: the ear of the heart. Ausculta: one word, and a life built on it. That's today, done.

1113.title: Stability
1113.hook: Benedictines vow to stay in one community for life
1113.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns make a vow of stability that ties them to a particular community; Benedictine oblates living outside the monastery can take stability as a call to stay faithful to their own family, parish and place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word of Benedict's Rule: listen. Your line was the ear of the heart.

A new monk stands in the chapel in front of the whole community. In his hand is a promise he has written out himself, and he lays it on the altar. Benedict's Rule says what goes in it. He promises obedience. He promises to keep turning his life toward God. And he promises something that sounds, to modern ears, almost impossible. He promises to stay. Not to stay a monk anywhere things feel right. Here, with these brothers, under this roof. No moving on when the abbot gets on his nerves or the brother in the next stall hums off key. The Rule's Latin word for that promise: stabilitas.

Stabilitas. Stability. To see why Benedict cared, look at his very first chapter. He describes different kinds of monks, and the ones he's hardest on are the wanderers. They drift from monastery to monastery, a few days here, a few days there, never settling, always guests. In the Rule's picture, they follow their own wishes and never stay long enough for anyone to know them. Benedict's answer is the vow to stay. Later, after a long list of what he calls the tools of the spiritual craft, things like don't return evil for evil, love your enemies, don't give up on God's mercy, he says where those tools get used. The workshop, he says, is the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the community. That's the surprise. Stability isn't a reward for being holy. It's the workbench. In this picture, patience gets learned with people you can't leave, and forgiveness gets tested by staying near the person you need to forgive. Move on every time it gets hard, and the tools never touch the wood. There's an old line in the Bible that sounds like this vow, though it comes from a different story. Ruth, a widow, refuses to leave her mother-in-law, and says, "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge." Stability is that kind of loyalty, given to a place and a people.

Sit where you are and notice the urge to move, to check the phone, shift your weight, get up for something, and don't follow it. Then bring to mind one place, one job, one relationship you'd like to walk out of today, and picture yourself staying a little longer, feet on the floor, without fixing anything; if you pray, bring that place to God by name. Staying never means staying where you're being hurt: if you're in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Stabilitas. The Benedictine promise to stay with one community, so that the hard work of love has somewhere to happen.
Your line: stay. In Benedict's picture, the workbench is the place you didn't leave. Until tomorrow.
